lesson.title: Monohybrid Crosses: Predicting the Inheritance of a Single Trait
lesson.summary: A monohybrid cross tracks the inheritance of a single gene between two parents, and a Punnett square lets us predict the exact genotype and phenotype ratios that will appear among their offspring.
lesson.body:
A monohybrid cross is a genetic cross that examines the inheritance of just one gene at a time. The name comes from mono, meaning one, and hybrid, meaning an individual heterozygous for that gene. The classic version of this cross, used as the running example throughout the last several chapters, breeds two individuals that are each heterozygous for the same gene, a Pp by Pp cross for pea flower color. Every worked example so far in this unit has, in fact, been a monohybrid cross, now formally named.

It is worth walking through the full method one more time, start to finish, using that same flower color trait, with P as the dominant purple allele and p as the recessive white allele. Cross a Pp mother with a Pp father. By the law of segregation, each parent produces P and p gametes in equal, 1 to 1 proportion. To predict the offspring, line up the mother's two possible gametes, P and p, across the top of a small grid, and the father's two possible gametes, P and p, down the side. Filling in the four resulting boxes gives: P from the mother with P from the father produces PP, P from the mother with p from the father produces Pp, p from the mother with P from the father produces Pp, and p from the mother with p from the father produces pp. Reading off the genotypes gives a ratio of 1 PP to 2 Pp to 1 pp. Because P is dominant, both PP and Pp show the purple phenotype, while only pp shows white, giving a phenotype ratio of 3 purple to 1 white.

It is worth being explicit about why this simple grid actually works as a prediction tool. Each parent contributes one allele to each offspring at random, with a 1 in 2 chance of contributing P and a 1 in 2 chance of contributing p, and fertilization combines one randomly-selected gamete from each parent. The Punnett square is really just a way of laying out all four equally likely combinations at once, each box representing a 1 in 4 chance, rather than working out that probability by hand for every possible outcome. That is why the 3 to 1 phenotype ratio shows up so reliably whenever two individuals heterozygous for the same completely dominant gene are crossed.

Not every monohybrid cross uses two heterozygous parents, either. A cross between a heterozygous individual and a homozygous recessive individual, Pp by pp, is also a monohybrid cross, and it produces a different, equally predictable result, half the offspring Pp and purple, half pp and white, a 1 to 1 phenotype ratio, which is exactly the logic behind the test cross described in the previous chapter. And a cross between two homozygous parents, a true breeding purple plant, PP, and a true breeding white plant, pp, produces offspring that are uniformly Pp and therefore uniformly purple, exactly the result Mendel obtained in his own original pea crosses before he then bred those purple F1 plants together to reveal the 3 to 1 ratio in the following generation. Across all of these variations, the monohybrid cross is really just the law of segregation, and the concepts of dominance, genotype, phenotype, and homozygosity built on top of it, turned into a concrete predictive tool for a single gene at a time. Extend that same logic to two genes at once, tracked on different chromosomes, and it becomes the law of independent assortment covered earlier in this unit.
